title: Count the cost (Luke 14:25–33)
hookLine: a builder sits down to reckon before building a tower

cards: On the edge of town sits a half-built house. The foundation poured, the frame up, and then nothing. Weeds in the yard, plywood going gray, a for-sale sign that's been there three summers.
The house tells its own story: somebody started and ran out of money. Jesus has great crowds walking with him on the road now. You'd think he'd be glad.
Instead he turns around and says something that sounds almost designed to thin the crowd.

teach.b: First the hard sentence. If anyone comes to me and hates not his father and mother, and wife and children, and brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. It's meant to stop you.
Matthew's Gospel helps here: it gives the saying as, he that loves father or mother more than me.
So readers hear hate as a way of speaking by contrast: loving one thing so much less than another that it looks like hate beside it. Jesus isn't canceling the commandment to honor your parents.

He's asking what comes first. Then two pictures. "For which of you having a mind to build a tower, doth not first sit down, and reckon the charges that are necessary, whether he have wherewithal to finish it."
Otherwise he lays the foundation, can't finish, and everyone laughs: this man began to build and was not able to finish.
Second picture: a king with ten thousand soldiers hears another king is coming with twenty thousand. Doesn't he sit down first and think? If he can't win, he sends an embassy and asks for peace.
Then the conclusion: every one of you that does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple.
Jesus isn't hiding the price to close the sale.

teach.h: SIT DOWN, AND RECKON THE CHARGES.
teach.b: He tells the crowd: sit down first, and count it. And notice the word sit. Both the builder and the king sit down.
In both pictures, deciding is done slowly, sitting down, with the numbers in front of you.

how: Catholics preparing for baptism, marriage, ordination or religious vows go through a period of formation and discernment, so that, as Luke puts it, they sit down and count the cost before they promise.

o: to announce something a second time aloud
to sign a formal letter quitting a job
to give up whatever would come before him

games.q: count the cost — tap the pairs.
p: sits down to reckon the charges
this man began and could not finish

s: Jesus is telling people to hate their families
Matthew's version says loves father or mother more than me: hate here means love less.
the builder and the king both sit down before acting
Luke uses the same picture for both: sit first, then decide.
Jesus hid the cost of discipleship to draw bigger crowds
he turned to the crowds and told them the cost up front.

games.q: you're a king with ten thousand soldiers. a king with twenty thousand is marching toward you. what do you do first?
o: sit down and consider whether you can win.
double your army by any means.
games.why: Jesus says he sits down first, and if he can't win, sends an embassy while the other king is still far away and asks for peace.

practice: Pick one thing you've said yes to, or are about to, a job, a relationship, a ministry, a promise, and sit with it the way the builder sits with his plans.
Name honestly what it will take, time, money, sleep, pride, and ask whether you have enough to finish, and what would help. If you pray, ask for wisdom and for what you lack.

wordCard.voice: Renounce. Jesus' warning to the crowds: sit down like a builder or a king and reckon what following him will take before you begin. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: sit down and reckon. No hidden price, no fine print. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: For which of you having a mind to build a tower, doth not first sit down, and reckon the charges that are necessary, whether he have wherewithal to finish it.
